## TL;DR

The second review identified that the task drawer still had two gaps despite the initial running-checks implementation: persisted handoff state could not reach the status branch that rendered it, and the progress bar was not reliably visible when the server reported no numeric progress or when only a local check slot was held. I corrected the status derivation and rendering, and preserved the existing detailed check-run information when a run is available. The scoped UI regressions and full `repoos check` passed. The change is ready for review round 3.

## Work and rationale

The task’s central requirement is that the UI reflect server ownership of a handoff, including after a reload or when the handoff was initiated through the CLI. A page cannot depend on having witnessed the `handoff:*` SSE event: opening the page later means there may be no in-memory event, and the check-history endpoint may still have no run row. The UI therefore needs to combine the persisted handoff status with live check-run and local-slot state. When the server says a handoff is running, that is enough to show “running checks” and suppress hints that infer a stall from agent silence.

Round 2 showed that the drawer’s status summary was not consistently allowing the persisted handoff state into its running-check branch. I updated the summary so server handoff activity participates in `checksRunning` before the confirmation-only state, making the running label reachable for a reload with no check row. The drawer uses the handoff step and elapsed time in that state. The existing running check row path still presents the check’s scope, machine and detailed progress text; this matters because the general handoff label should not erase useful run-specific detail.

The progress element now remains present when the drawer has live check progress, a persisted running handoff, or a local slot held for the task. When a numeric percentage is unavailable, its value is omitted so the browser renders an indeterminate bar. The accompanying label uses “Starting…” when there is no more specific information, the handoff step when known, or the actual check progress label when available. This keeps the panel visibly active without inventing a percentage or duration.

I added a regression for the reload case: the fixture has a running server handoff at `verify`, no check-history row, and no live SSE event. The assertions cover the running label with elapsed duration, absence of quiet/stuck warnings, and the indeterminate progress bar. Assertions also cover the held-slot progress state. The shot-preview fixture guard remains in place so synthetic task IDs do not trigger unrelated summary or handoff-status requests during UI verification.

The original investigation found that the empty `runs` list was possible because the CLI-requested handoff status is separate from the check-run history returned by the checks endpoint. A server handoff can be in `check` while that history has no corresponding row, so using run history as the sole hydration source loses valid activity. The implementation represents that distinction in the UI rather than assuming that a missing run means no check is in progress.

## Approaches tried

I first followed the review’s suggestion to merge the drawer with the current main branch. The merge produced overlapping edits in `TaskDrawer.vue` and the task’s own work file. Because this runner session is instructed not to stage or commit, I aborted the merge instead of resolving it through a manual merge commit. I then reconciled the relevant drawer behavior directly: retained the task’s handoff and progress work, and adopted the shared shot-preview fetch guard pattern needed by the current tree. Unrelated changes to engineering-report display were not part of this task’s behavior and were not copied into the feature change.

I ran the focused drawer/status/card test selection through the repository’s `bun run test` wrapper. All 28 selected tests passed. A direct `bunx vitest` invocation initially bypassed the repository setup and failed during UI environment initialization (`window is not defined`); it did not represent a product regression, so I used the supported wrapper for meaningful test results.

The full `repoos check` initially exposed a compile-time issue in a test fixture and then two expectation/branch issues in the drawer. I corrected those and reran the complete gate. A later remote validation also exposed that preserving only the handoff status text hid the existing detailed check-run lines; I narrowed the branch so those details remain when a check run is present. The final full gate completed successfully, including remote tests, rendered contrast validation, UI smoke, docs and auxiliary package checks, and the local safety guards.

## Challenges and blockers

The most important edge case is that “running” has more than one source: a server-owned handoff, an active check-run record, or a local slot held for the task. Those signals provide different amounts of detail. The implementation keeps the status decision shared but makes the display tolerate missing percentage and run history. In particular, omitting the progress value is necessary for a native indeterminate progress element; forcing a default numeric value would falsely imply measured progress.

The review’s merge request overlapped a broad current-main drawer change. A full merge was not completed because the managed task workflow disallows manual staging and committing in this session. The relevant current-tree fetch guard and drawer behavior were reconciled in the task branch, and the full gate ran against that resulting tree. RepoOS will perform its normal server-side validation and commit when the handoff is requested.

One earlier verification attempt timed out during server-side finalization, and another UI verification run used a synthetic task ID that returned 404s. Those failures led to review of fixture request behavior and the shot target. In this continuation, the focused tests passed and the final local `repoos check` reported “All checks passed” with no failed steps. No live preview was requested; UI verification was performed by the repository’s managed check pipeline.

## Key learnings

The UI must treat handoff status and check-run history as complementary server data. An empty run list is not evidence that the handoff has stopped. Persisted status must be part of the initial hydrated state so reloads and second devices behave like clients that saw the SSE event.

Progress UI should communicate known state faithfully. A check can be running without an available percentage, and a local slot can establish activity before a run row appears. Showing an indeterminate progress bar with an accurate step label makes that state visible without fabricating progress. Run-specific labels and metadata should remain when present.

For UI regressions, exercise the repository’s own test wrapper and realistic shot fixtures. Synthetic task fixtures can otherwise generate irrelevant network errors, while a missing declared highlight is a hard verification failure. The final check is the useful evidence: it exercised the full configured gate and completed with no failed steps.
